Chapter One: Growing Up Different and Learning to Hide
You know, childhood can feel a lot like a never-ending audition. There's this constant pressure to fit in, to be accepted. Picture a quiet suburb in Illinois—a place where a tall, kinda awkward kid with a voice that could fill a room just wanted to blend in, even though everything about her made her stand out.
Family dinners were loud and full of laughter. There was always someone joking or teasing, but if you listened closely, you’d hear an undercurrent—a quiet anxiety about being too much, too loud, or just too different. At school, it always seemed like there was this unwritten rulebook about how to fit in. The popular kids just seemed to know what to do, almost effortlessly. There was this deep longing to be part of their circle, to get that invite, but also a little rebellious spark that refused to play by all their rules. That constant tug-of-war—wanting to belong, but not able to hide what made her unique—really shaped those early years.
Home was both a safe haven and a puzzle. The parents? Loving, sure, but also pretty traditional. They offered support in their own way, but there were things they just didn’t quite get—especially the battles happening inside. There was love, yes, but also this subtle nudge to follow a certain path... to be “normal.” And with siblings in the mix, there was always this blend of camaraderie and competition—everyone trying to find their own little corner in the family story.
Early on, humor became the go-to defense. Making people laugh was like wearing armor. If you could get someone to giggle, you could distract them from your own insecurities. Imitating teachers, neighbors, even family members? That got applause and, for a moment, it felt like belonging. But the laughs could sting, too. Sometimes, being the funny one just made the feeling of being on the outside even stronger—more class clown than close friend.
Then came adolescence, and everything got trickier. While other kids navigated crushes and dances, there was this growing sense that things weren’t following the script. The world had all these ideas about how girls should act, who they should like, what they should want. Not fitting into that mold brought on a mix of shame and confusion, and that’s when the real hiding started. Masking feelings, playing roles, just hoping no one would notice what was really going on underneath.
Sometimes, the urge to just disappear was overwhelming. But at the same time, there was this deep need to be seen. It’s funny how those two things can live side by side. That’s why the stage became such a lifeline—joining the school choir, auditioning for plays, grabbing every chance to perform. Up there, being different wasn’t just okay—it was a superpower. In the spotlight, quirks turned into strengths, and the applause felt like real, genuine acceptance.
Of course, once the lights faded, all those old worries came rushing back. There was always this calculation: how much of yourself do you show, and how much do you keep hidden? Friendships were built on shared secrets and inside jokes, but the biggest secret always stayed locked up tight. The fear of being rejected was just too strong, shaping every choice and every conversation.
Looking back, those years were a crash course in resilience. All that struggling to fit in, the pain of feeling so different, the energy it took just to hide—believe it or not, it all laid the groundwork for a deeper sense of self later on. Most people have no idea how exhausting it is to pretend, or how freeing it is when you finally stop. But back then? Embracing what set you apart felt impossible. The best hope was to just keep performing, keep hiding, and wait for that one unexpected, happy accident that might change everything.
